title: Coconut Water for a Hangover: Does It Beat Gatorade or Pedialyte?
excerpt: Is coconut water good for a hangover? What it really contains, why sodium matters more than potassium after drinking, what the 2012 study found, and when to pick Pedialyte instead.
metaDescription: Is coconut water good for a hangover? Why sodium beats potassium, what the 2012 study really found, and when Pedialyte or Gatorade work better.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** coconut water can help with the thirsty, dried-out part of a hangover, and it's a perfectly reasonable thing to drink the morning after. But it isn't the rehydration powerhouse its marketing suggests. Its strong suit is potassium, and the electrolyte you most need to replace after drinking is sodium, which coconut water usually has much less of. If you had a light night and you like the taste, go ahead. If you had a heavy night, were sick, or sweated a lot, an oral rehydration drink like Pedialyte (or coconut water with a pinch of salt and some food) will do the job better.

**The quick rules:** Drink something with sodium in it, not just water. Coconut water counts as a mild option, not a strong one. Pair it with salty food, or add a small pinch of salt. Don't drink it by the liter if you have kidney disease or take medicines that raise potassium. And remember that rehydration only treats part of a hangover. It won't fix the headache from acetaldehyde, the poor sleep, or the inflammation.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general nutrition research in plain language. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** you can't keep fluids down for more than a day, you have signs of serious dehydration (dizziness when you stand, confusion, very dark urine or very little urine), you have kidney disease or heart failure, or you take medicines that raise potassium levels (such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, or other potassium-sparing diuretics). In an emergency, call 911.

## What Coconut Water Actually Contains

Coconut water is the clear liquid inside young green coconuts. It isn't coconut milk, which is made by blending the white flesh with water and is high in fat. Coconut water is mostly water, with a little natural sugar and a mix of minerals.

Here's roughly what you get in one cup (about 240 ml, or 8 ounces) of plain, unsweetened coconut water. Treat these as ballpark figures, because the numbers swing a lot depending on the coconut's age, where it was grown, and how the brand processes it:

| Per cup (about 240 ml) | Plain coconut water (typical range) |
|---|---|
| Calories | about 45 to 60 |
| Sugar | about 6 to 12 g, all naturally occurring in unsweetened versions |
| Potassium | about 400 to 700 mg |
| Sodium | about 30 to 250 mg, and often near the low end in packaged brands |
| Magnesium | a modest amount, roughly 15 to 60 mg |

Two things stand out. First, the potassium is genuinely high. A cup of coconut water can carry as much potassium as a banana. Second, the sodium is low and unpredictable. Some brands list only a few dozen milligrams per serving, which is a small fraction of what a proper rehydration drink contains.

That gap is the whole story of this article. So it's worth understanding why sodium, not potassium, is the electrolyte that matters most after a night of drinking.

## Why Drinking Dehydrates You (and What You Actually Lose)

Alcohol makes you pee more than the fluid you drink would explain. It does this by suppressing vasopressin, a hormone (also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of that signal, your kidneys let more water go. This is well established and is described in the hangover guidance from the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.

The fluid you lose isn't pure water. Urine carries sodium, potassium, and other salts with it. On a typical night out, you may also lose more through:

- **Sweat.** Dancing, a hot bar, a summer wedding. Sweat is salty because it carries a lot of sodium and comparatively little potassium.
- **Vomiting.** If the night ended badly, you lost fluid plus stomach contents that carry both sodium and potassium.
- **Not eating.** Many people drink without a proper meal, so the sodium they'd normally get from food never comes in.

When you're short on fluid, sodium is what helps your body keep the water you drink in your bloodstream instead of sending it straight back out. Sodium is the main salt in the fluid outside your cells, and that's the fluid that drops when you're dehydrated. Potassium mostly lives inside your cells. It matters, but your body usually loses less of it on a night out, and a normal meal tends to replace it.

### The sugar-and-salt trick your gut uses

There's another reason sodium matters. Your small intestine absorbs water fastest when sodium and glucose arrive together, because they share a transport system in the gut wall. Pull sodium and sugar in together and water follows them. This is the science behind oral rehydration solutions (ORS), the low-cost salt-and-sugar drinks the World Health Organization recommends for dehydration from diarrheal illness. It's one of the most important medical discoveries of the last century, and it's why drugstore products like Pedialyte are built the way they are.

Coconut water has the sugar part of that pairing. What it usually lacks is enough sodium to make the system work at full speed.

## Coconut Water vs Sports Drinks vs Pedialyte: The Real Numbers

Here's how coconut water lines up against the two drinks people most often reach for. Figures are approximate per 12 ounces (about 355 ml) and vary by flavor and formula, so check the label on what you actually buy:

| Per 12 oz (about 355 ml) | Plain coconut water | Regular Gatorade | Pedialyte (classic) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | roughly 45 to 370 mg, usually low | about 160 mg | about 370 mg |
| Potassium | roughly 600 to 1,000 mg | about 50 mg | about 280 mg |
| Sugar | roughly 9 to 18 g | about 21 g | about 9 g |
| Designed for | nothing in particular; it's a natural drink | athletes mid-workout | rehydration during illness |

A few things jump out:

- **Coconut water wins on potassium by a mile.** It has far more than either Gatorade or Pedialyte.
- **Coconut water usually loses on sodium.** Most packaged coconut water has less sodium than Gatorade and far less than Pedialyte. That's backwards from what you want for rehydration.
- **It sits in the middle on sugar.** Less than regular Gatorade, often similar to or a bit more than Pedialyte.

For a full side-by-side of the two drugstore options, see our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade hangover comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover). The short version of that page is that Pedialyte wins on rehydration quality because it carries more sodium and less sugar. Coconut water would land below both of them on the measure that matters most.

### Coconut water vs Gatorade

If you're choosing between these two for a hangover, it's closer than coconut water fans think. Gatorade has more sodium; coconut water has much more potassium and less sugar. For a mild hangover, either one is fine and the better choice is whichever you'll actually drink. For a heavy night or a lot of sweating, Gatorade's extra sodium gives it a slight edge for rehydration, while coconut water is the gentler pick if a sugary sports drink turns your stomach.

### Coconut water vs Pedialyte

Pedialyte is the better rehydration tool, and it isn't especially close. It's built on oral rehydration science, with a sodium level designed to drive absorption and replace losses. Coconut water wasn't designed for anything. If you were vomiting, had a very long night, or feel dizzy when you stand up, reach for an oral rehydration drink rather than coconut water.

### Coconut water vs plain water

Coconut water is a modest step up from plain water because it adds some electrolytes and a little sugar. For a light hangover after a couple of drinks with dinner, plain water and a normal breakfast will usually do just as well. The one case where plain water alone falls short is when you've lost a lot of fluid and eaten nothing, because water without any salt replaces volume but not electrolytes.

## What the Research Actually Shows: The 2012 Study, Honestly

Almost every article that recommends coconut water for hangovers leans on the same piece of evidence: a small study published in 2012 in the *Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition* by Kalman and colleagues. It's worth knowing what it did and didn't find, because it gets stretched a long way.

**What they did.** A small group of exercise-trained young men (around a dozen) exercised until they had lost a modest amount of body weight through sweat. They then rehydrated on separate occasions with plain water, coconut water, coconut water made from concentrate, or a sports drink, and the researchers measured how well they rehydrated and how they performed on a follow-up exercise test.

**What they found.** All the drinks rehydrated the men reasonably well, and the differences in hydration and performance between them were small. Coconut water did about as well as the sports drink. Some participants found coconut water more filling and reported more bloating or stomach upset after drinking it in larger volumes.

**What that does and doesn't tell you about hangovers:**

- **It wasn't a hangover study.** The men were dehydrated by exercise, not alcohol. Nobody drank anything alcoholic.
- **It was small.** A dozen people can show that something is in the same ballpark, but it can't detect modest differences or tell you how it works for everyone.
- **"About as good as a sports drink" is a modest claim.** As the table above shows, sports drinks themselves aren't optimized for rehydration. Matching Gatorade is not the same as matching an oral rehydration solution.
- **The stomach issue is relevant.** If coconut water can feel heavy in a fit, well-rested athlete, it may sit even less comfortably on a queasy hungover stomach when you gulp a lot of it.

There's a little more research in the same vein. An earlier study from Malaysia (Saat and colleagues, 2002, in the *Journal of Physiological Anthropology and Applied Human Science*) also found that fresh young coconut water rehydrated people after exercise about as well as plain water or a sports drink, and that some participants found it easier to drink in large amounts. Researchers in the same group also tested coconut water with added sodium and found it performed well, which tells you something: when scientists wanted to make coconut water a better rehydration drink, they added salt.

Nobody, as far as we know, has run a controlled trial of coconut water as a hangover remedy. So the honest summary is this: coconut water is a decent everyday fluid that rehydrates about as well as a sports drink after exercise. There's no direct evidence that it treats hangovers any better than other fluids do.

## Why Rehydration Only Fixes Part of a Hangover

This matters more than which drink you choose. Dehydration is real, and it explains some hangover symptoms: thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness when you stand, and some of the headache and tiredness. But researchers who have measured hydration markers in hungover people have generally found that dehydration doesn't track closely with how bad the hangover feels. In other words, you can rehydrate fully and still feel terrible.

The rest of a hangover comes from other sources:

- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that contributes to nausea, flushing, and the poisoned feeling. No drink washes it out faster.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, which may explain some of the achy, flu-like feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep, then fragments your sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Low blood sugar and stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and can affect blood sugar, especially if you didn't eat.
- **Congeners.** Darker drinks contain more by-products of fermentation that seem to make hangovers worse for some people. Our upcoming guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes into this.

So coconut water can make you feel less parched. It won't touch the headache that comes from acetaldehyde or the fog from a bad night's sleep. For a broader look at what does and doesn't help, see our [science-based guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide).

## When Coconut Water Is a Good Choice

Coconut water isn't a bad pick. It just has a specific lane. It fits well when:

- **The hangover is mild.** A few drinks, some thirst, a dull morning. You don't need a medical-grade rehydration drink, and coconut water is pleasant and easy to sip.
- **You'll be eating too.** A salty breakfast (eggs, toast with butter, a bowl of soup, a bagel) supplies the sodium coconut water lacks. Together they make a solid combination.
- **Sugary sports drinks turn your stomach.** Some people find Gatorade too sweet first thing in the morning. Unsweetened coconut water is lighter.
- **You want something with no artificial sweeteners or dyes.** Plain coconut water is a whole-food drink, which some people prefer.
- **You're topping up through the day.** After the first glass of a proper electrolyte drink, coconut water is a fine way to keep fluids going.

## When to Choose Something Else

Reach for an oral rehydration drink, or at least something with more sodium, when:

- **You vomited.** You lost fluid and salts quickly, and coconut water's low sodium won't replace them well. Take small sips of an oral rehydration solution instead, and see a doctor if you can't keep anything down.
- **You had a long, heavy night with little food.** Bigger fluid deficit, no sodium from meals. This is where sodium matters most.
- **You were sweating a lot.** Sweat is salty, so sodium losses add up.
- **You feel dizzy when you stand up.** That's a sign your blood volume is low, which is exactly what sodium helps fix.

Our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares the electrolyte powders and oral rehydration products if you want options beyond Pedialyte.

### Who should be careful with coconut water

Coconut water's high potassium is fine for most healthy people, because healthy kidneys clear extra potassium easily. It's a different story if your kidneys don't work normally or you take medicines that make your body hold on to potassium. Examples include ACE inhibitors (like lisinopril), angiotensin receptor blockers (like losartan), spironolactone and other potassium-sparing diuretics, and some other prescription drugs. In those situations, drinking large amounts of coconut water could push potassium too high, which can affect heart rhythm. There are published medical case reports of dangerously high potassium after people drank large quantities of coconut water.

If any of that applies to you, ask your doctor or pharmacist before using coconut water as your go-to rehydration drink. A glass now and then is very different from a liter or two, but it's worth checking.

## How to Make Coconut Water Work Better for a Hangover

If you like coconut water and want to use it, a few small changes make it a much better rehydration drink:

1. **Add a pinch of salt.** A small pinch of table salt (roughly an eighth of a teaspoon) in a large glass adds a few hundred milligrams of sodium and moves coconut water closer to an oral rehydration drink. Taste it; it should taste slightly salty, not like seawater. More is not better.
2. **Eat something salty with it.** Toast, eggs, crackers, broth, or soup do the same job without changing the drink.
3. **Sip, don't chug.** Large volumes at once can upset a hungover stomach, which echoes what some participants reported in the 2012 study. A glass, then another 20 or 30 minutes later, works better.
4. **Buy plain and unsweetened.** Some coconut waters have added sugar or are blended with fruit juice. That adds sugar without adding sodium.
5. **Check the sodium on the label.** Brands vary widely. If you're choosing between two, the one with more sodium is the better rehydration pick.

That first tip is the most useful thing in this article. Coconut water's weak spot for rehydration is low sodium, and a pinch of salt fixes most of it for almost no cost.

## Coconut Water Before or While Drinking

Some people drink coconut water before going out, or alternate it with alcohol through the night. There's nothing wrong with that. Staying ahead on fluids is a sensible habit, and anything that slows how fast you drink alcohol helps. But coconut water doesn't do anything special to prevent a hangover, and it doesn't protect your liver or speed up how fast you clear alcohol.

When you drink electrolytes matters less than the fact that you're taking in fluids and food at all. Our guide to [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing in more detail. For a fuller pre-drinking plan, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) and our upcoming checklist on [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking).

### Is coconut water a good mixer?

Coconut water is a popular mixer with rum, vodka, and tequila, and it's a lighter choice than sugary sodas or juice. But mixing it into your drinks doesn't cancel out the alcohol. A coconut water and rum still contains the same amount of alcohol as a rum and cola, and the hangover risk comes from the alcohol. If anything, a pleasant, easy-drinking mixer can make it easier to drink more than you meant to. Count drinks the same way you would with any other mixer.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

On this site we write a lot about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's sold as a supplement to take around drinking. It's worth being clear about how it relates to coconut water, because they do completely different jobs.

Coconut water is a fluid. At most, it helps with the dehydration part of a hangover. DHM is studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol: early research, mostly in animals and lab settings, suggests it may support alcohol metabolism and protect the liver, but the human evidence is limited and it shouldn't be treated as a proven hangover cure. Neither one replaces the other, and neither makes heavy drinking safe.

If you're curious about DHM, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains the research and how people typically take it. One straightforward option we review is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a plain DHM capsule without the extra blends. You'd still want fluids, food, and sleep the next morning either way.

## A Simple Morning-After Plan

If you woke up with a hangover and coconut water in the fridge, here's a sensible order of things:

1. **Start with a glass of fluid that has some sodium.** Coconut water with a pinch of salt, an oral rehydration drink, or a sports drink.
2. **Eat something.** Salty, gentle food helps with sodium, blood sugar, and an unsettled stomach.
3. **Keep sipping through the morning.** Aim for pale yellow urine as a rough sign you're catching up.
4. **Handle a headache carefully.** If you need a pain reliever, read up first, because the common ones each carry their own risks after drinking. Our pages on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) explain the trade-offs.
5. **Rest.** Sleep does more for the non-dehydration parts of a hangover than any drink.
6. **Know the warning signs.** Repeated vomiting, confusion, or being unable to keep fluids down for a day or more needs medical attention, not more coconut water.

If you're still struggling well into the next day, our upcoming guide to the [two-day hangover](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) explains why some hangovers drag on and what to do about it.

## The Bottom Line

Coconut water is a pleasant, natural drink that rehydrates about as well as a sports drink after exercise, based on small studies. It's high in potassium and usually low in sodium, which is the opposite of what you most need after a night of drinking. For a mild hangover, it's a fine choice, especially with salty food or a pinch of salt added. For a rough night with vomiting, heavy sweating, or dizziness, an oral rehydration drink like Pedialyte is the better tool. And no drink, coconut water included, fixes the parts of a hangover that come from acetaldehyde, inflammation, and bad sleep.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is coconut water good for a hangover?**

It helps with the dehydration part of a hangover, like thirst, dry mouth, and some of the tiredness, and it's easy on the stomach for many people. But it's high in potassium and usually low in sodium, which is the electrolyte you most need to replace after drinking. For a mild hangover it's a fine choice, especially with salty food. For a heavy night, an oral rehydration drink like Pedialyte works better.

**Is coconut water better than Gatorade for a hangover?**

Not clearly. Coconut water has much more potassium and less sugar, while regular Gatorade has more sodium. A small 2012 study found coconut water rehydrated exercising men about as well as a sports drink, but it wasn't a hangover study. For a mild hangover, pick whichever you'll actually drink. If you need serious rehydration, a higher-sodium oral rehydration drink beats both.

**Is coconut water or Pedialyte better for a hangover?**

Pedialyte is the better rehydration drink. It's built on oral rehydration science, with roughly 370 mg of sodium per 12 ounces and modest sugar, which helps your gut absorb water quickly. Most packaged coconut water has far less sodium. Coconut water is fine for a light hangover, but if you vomited, sweated a lot, or feel dizzy when standing, choose Pedialyte or a similar oral rehydration drink.

**Should I drink coconut water before drinking alcohol?**

You can, and staying ahead on fluids is a sensible habit, but coconut water doesn't prevent hangovers. It doesn't speed up how fast you clear alcohol or protect your liver. Eating a real meal, pacing your drinks, and alternating alcohol with water or another non-alcoholic drink do more than any particular beverage.

**How much coconut water should I drink for a hangover?**

There's no set amount. A glass or two over the morning, sipped rather than chugged, alongside food is a reasonable approach for most healthy adults. Drinking a liter or more quickly can upset a queasy stomach. If you have kidney disease or take medicines that raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or spironolactone, ask your doctor before drinking large amounts.

**Can you add salt to coconut water for a hangover?**

Yes, and it's the single best way to improve it. A small pinch of table salt (roughly an eighth of a teaspoon) in a large glass adds a few hundred milligrams of sodium, which brings coconut water closer to an oral rehydration drink. It should taste slightly salty, not like seawater. Eating something salty alongside it works too.

**Is coconut water a good mixer to avoid a hangover?**

It's a lighter mixer than soda or sugary juice, but it doesn't reduce the alcohol in your drink, and alcohol is what causes the hangover. A rum and coconut water has the same alcohol as a rum and cola. Count drinks the same way you would with any other mixer.
